concept_html:
A test is worth writing if it fails when the code is wrong. For data code, most bugs sit at the edges: empty input, missing values, zero denominators, one row, duplicate keys. Test those on purpose.

With pytest 9, a test is a function whose name starts with test_ and which uses plain assert:

import pytest


def test_share_zero_total_is_none():
    assert share(3, 0) is None


@pytest.mark.parametrize(("part", "total", "expected"), [(1, 4, 0.25), (0, 5, 0.0), (5, 5, 1.0)])
def test_share_values(part, total, expected):
    assert share(part, total) == expected

Habits that make tests catch bugs:

  • Test pure functions (lesson B2-L1). No files, clocks or databases, so tests are fast and exact.
  • Build tiny, explicit inputs in the test itself: three rows, written out. A reader sees the input and the expected answer together.
  • One behaviour per test, named for it: test_zero_total_returns_none, not test_share_2.
  • Compare DataFrames with pd.testing.assert_frame_equal. It checks values, dtypes, column order and index, and prints a clear difference.
  • Compare floats with pytest.approx when the value comes from arithmetic: assert mean == pytest.approx(0.3).
  • Use tmp_path for anything that writes files. pytest gives each test a fresh temporary directory.

Check that each test can fail. Break the code on purpose, once, and watch the test go red. A test that stays green whatever you do protects nothing. This course's own quality gate does the same: every seeded bug must fail its checker.

Run the tests in CI on every push (lesson A10-L3), and fix a failing test before merging anything else.

title: Unit tests for data code that catch real bugs
why_html: A share function had a test, assert share(1, 4) == 0.25, and 100% line coverage. The zero-total branch returned 0.0 instead of None. Dashboards showed empty segments as "0% of respondents", which the client read as a real finding. A four-word test, assert share(3, 0) is None, would have failed on the first run.
